notes.title: Circles · Formula sheet
notes.body:
The chapter at one glance. Each line links to its concept note.

- [[Equation of a circle]]: $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$; $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ has centre $(-g,-f)$, radius $\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}$
- [[Tangents & normals]]: $T=0$ at a point; $y=mx\pm r\sqrt{1+m^2}$ for slope $m$
- [[Chord of contact, polar & pole]]: chord of contact and polar are both $T=0$
- [[Chord with given midpoint]]: $T=S_1$
- [[Two circles: position, common tangents]]: compare $d=|C_1C_2|$ with $r_1+r_2$ and $|r_1-r_2|$
- [[Orthogonal circles, radical axis]]: $2(g_1g_2+f_1f_2)=c_1+c_2$; radical axis $S-S'=0$
- [[Family of circles]]: $S+\lambda S'=0$, $S+\lambda L=0$
- [[Locus & maximum/minimum]]: distances from a point to a circle lie between $|CP-r|$ and $CP+r$

Notation: $S=x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c$, $S_1=S(x_1,y_1)$, $T=xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)+c$.

notes.title: Equation of a circle
notes.body:
# Equation of a circle
A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance $r$ (radius) from a fixed point $C(h,k)$ (centre).

**Forms**
- Centre–radius: $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$
- General: $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$, centre $(-g,-f)$, radius $r=\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}$
- Diameter form, ends $(x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2)$: $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$
- Parametric: $x=h+r\cos\theta,\; y=k+r\sin\theta$

**When is a second-degree equation a circle?** $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+\dots=0$ is a circle only if $a=b\ne0$ and $h=0$ (no $xy$ term), and then $g^2+f^2-c\ge0$ after dividing by $a$.
- $g^2+f^2-c=0$: a point circle. $g^2+f^2-c<0$: no real circle.

**Example.** $x^2+y^2-4x+6y-12=0$: centre $(2,-3)$, $r=\sqrt{4+9+12}=5$.

**Common mistake:** forgetting to divide by the coefficient of $x^2$ before reading $g, f, c$.

Next: [[Tangents & normals]] · Back to [[Circles · Formula sheet]]

notes.title: Tangents & normals
notes.body:
# Tangents & normals
A line touches the circle when the distance from the centre equals the radius: $\ell=r$.

**Tangent at a point $(x_1,y_1)$ on the circle**
- $x^2+y^2=r^2$: $\;xx_1+yy_1=r^2$
- General circle: $T=0$, i.e. $xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)+c=0$

**Tangent with slope $m$**
- $x^2+y^2=r^2$: $\;y=mx\pm r\sqrt{1+m^2}$
- Centre $(h,k)$: $\;y-k=m(x-h)\pm r\sqrt{1+m^2}$

**Pair of tangents from an outside point $P(x_1,y_1)$:** $\;S\,S_1=T^2$.
- Length of tangent: $PT=\sqrt{S_1}$ (this is why $S_1>0$ means $P$ is outside).
- Angle between the two tangents: $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{2r\sqrt{S_1}}{S_1-r^2}\right|$

**Normal** at $(x_1,y_1)$ always passes through the centre: $\;y-y_1=\dfrac{y_1+f}{x_1+g}(x-x_1)$.

**Power of a point:** $S_1=|CP|^2-r^2$: positive outside, zero on, negative inside.

**Common mistake:** using $T=0$ for a point that is *not* on the circle. Then $T=0$ is the chord of contact, not a tangent: see [[Chord of contact, polar & pole]].

See also [[Chord of contact, polar & pole]] · [[Equation of a circle]]

notes.title: Chord of contact, polar & pole
notes.body:
# Chord of contact, polar & pole
From an outside point $P(x_1,y_1)$ draw the two tangents; the chord joining the points of contact is the **chord of contact**:
$$T=0:\quad xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)+c=0$$

**Polar and pole**
- The polar of any point $P(x_1,y_1)$ (inside, on or outside) is the line $T=0$.
- The pole of a line is the point whose polar it is.
- If $P$ lies on the polar of $Q$, then $Q$ lies on the polar of $P$ (conjugate points).

**Length of the chord of contact** (tangent length $\ell=\sqrt{S_1}$): $\;\dfrac{2\ell r}{\sqrt{r^2+\ell^2}}$

**Example.** Chord of contact from $(3,4)$ to $x^2+y^2=9$: $3x+4y=9$.

**Common mistake:** mixing up $T=0$ (chord of contact / polar) with $T=S_1$ ([[Chord with given midpoint]]).

See also [[Tangents & normals]]

notes.title: Chord with given midpoint
notes.body:
# Chord with given midpoint
The chord of $S=0$ whose midpoint is $M(x_1,y_1)$ is
$$T=S_1$$
i.e. $xx_1+yy_1+g(x+x_1)+f(y+y_1)=x_1^2+y_1^2+2gx_1+2fy_1$.

**Why:** the chord is perpendicular to $CM$ and passes through $M$.

**Length of a chord** at distance $p$ from the centre: $2\sqrt{r^2-p^2}$.

**Locus questions:** "midpoints of chords that pass through a fixed point / subtend a right angle / have fixed length" all start from $T=S_1$, then use the given condition.

**Example.** Chord of $x^2+y^2=25$ with midpoint $(1,2)$: $x+2y=5$.

See also [[Chord of contact, polar & pole]] · [[Locus & maximum/minimum]]

notes.title: Two circles: position, common tangents
notes.body:
# Two circles: position, common tangents
Let $d=|C_1C_2|$.

- Separate: $d>r_1+r_2$ → **4** common tangents
- Touch externally: $d=r_1+r_2$ → **3**
- Intersect: $|r_1-r_2|<d<r_1+r_2$ → **2**
- Touch internally: $d=|r_1-r_2|$ → **1**
- One inside the other: $d<|r_1-r_2|$ → **0**

**Angle of intersection** $\theta$: $\;\cos\theta=\left|\dfrac{r_1^2+r_2^2-d^2}{2r_1r_2}\right|$

**Centres of similitude:** the direct common tangents meet at the point dividing $C_1C_2$ externally in $r_1:r_2$; the transverse ones meet at the point dividing it internally in $r_1:r_2$.

**Common mistake:** counting tangents without checking the touching cases ($d$ exactly equal).

See also [[Orthogonal circles, radical axis]]

notes.title: Orthogonal circles, radical axis
notes.body:
# Orthogonal circles, radical axis
**Orthogonal circles** cut at right angles: $d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2$, i.e.
$$2(g_1g_2+f_1f_2)=c_1+c_2$$

**Radical axis** of $S=0$ and $S'=0$: $\;S-S'=0$, a straight line
$$2(g_1-g_2)x+2(f_1-f_2)y+c_1-c_2=0$$
- From any point on it, the tangents to both circles are equal.
- It is perpendicular to the line of centres.
- For intersecting circles it is the common chord.

**Radical centre:** the radical axes of three circles (centres not collinear) meet at one point; the circle centred there with radius = tangent length is orthogonal to all three.

**Common mistake:** forgetting to make the coefficients of $x^2$ equal to 1 in both circles before $S-S'$.

See also [[Family of circles]] · [[Two circles: position, common tangents]]

notes.title: Family of circles
notes.body:
# Family of circles
Write the family, then use the one extra condition to find $\lambda$.

- Through the intersection of circles $S=0,\;S'=0$: $\;S+\lambda S'=0$ ($\lambda\ne-1$; $\lambda=-1$ gives the radical axis)
- Through the intersection of circle $S=0$ and line $L=0$: $\;S+\lambda L=0$
- Touching line $L=0$ at the point $(x_1,y_1)$: $\;(x-x_1)^2+(y-y_1)^2+\lambda L=0$
- Through two points $A,B$: $\;(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)+\lambda L=0$, with $L$ the line $AB$
- Circumcircle of the triangle formed by $L_1,L_2,L_3$: $\;L_1L_2+\lambda L_2L_3+\mu L_1L_3=0$ with coeff. of $xy=0$ and coeff. of $x^2$ = coeff. of $y^2$

**Example.** Circle through the intersection of $x^2+y^2=4$ and $x+y=1$ passing through the origin: $S+\lambda L=0$ at $(0,0)$ gives $-4-\lambda=0$, so $x^2+y^2-4x-4y=0$.

See also [[Orthogonal circles, radical axis]]

notes.title: Locus & maximum/minimum
notes.body:
# Locus & maximum/minimum
**Distance from a point $P$ to a circle** (centre $C$, radius $r$):
- least $=|CP-r|$, greatest $=CP+r$, both along the line $CP$.

**Parametric point** $(h+r\cos\theta,\,k+r\sin\theta)$ turns max–min questions into $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta$, whose range is $[-\sqrt{a^2+b^2},\sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$.

**Locus routine**
1. Call the moving point $(h,k)$.
2. Write the condition (midpoint, right angle, tangents at fixed angle…) using $T=0$, $T=S_1$ or $SS_1=T^2$.
3. Eliminate the parameter, then replace $h,k$ by $x,y$.

**Classic:** tangents from $P$ to $x^2+y^2=r^2$ at right angles $\Rightarrow$ $P$ lies on the director circle $x^2+y^2=2r^2$.

See also [[Chord with given midpoint]] · [[Tangents & normals]]

notes.title: Quadratic Equations · Formula sheet
notes.body:
The chapter at one glance.

- [[Nature of roots & discriminant]]: $D=b^2-4ac$
- [[Sum & product of roots, symmetric functions]]: $\alpha+\beta=-\tfrac ba,\;\alpha\beta=\tfrac ca$
- [[Forming equations, transformed roots]]: $x^2-(\text{sum})x+\text{product}=0$
- [[Common roots]]: $(c_1a_2-c_2a_1)^2=(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)$
- [[Location of roots]]: sign of $f(k)$, vertex, $D$
- [[Graph & sign of a quadratic, range]]: $y=a\left(x+\tfrac b{2a}\right)^2-\tfrac D{4a}$
- [[Higher-degree polynomials]]: Vieta for degree $n$, Newton's sums
- [[Reducible equations (modulus, log, exponential)]]: substitute, then check the domain
- [[Quadratic inequalities & parameters]]: $ax^2+bx+c>0\;\forall x\iff a>0,\;D<0$

notes.title: Nature of roots & discriminant
notes.body:
# Nature of roots & discriminant
For $ax^2+bx+c=0$ ($a\ne0$): $\;\alpha,\beta=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt D}{2a}$, $D=b^2-4ac$.

**Real coefficients**
- $D>0$: real, distinct
- $D=0$: real, equal ($x=-\tfrac b{2a}$)
- $D<0$: non-real, a conjugate pair

**Rational coefficients:** $D$ a perfect square $\Rightarrow$ rational roots; irrational roots come in pairs $p\pm\sqrt q$.

**Integer coefficients, $a=1$:** a rational root must be an integer.

**Identity test:** if $ax^2+bx+c=0$ has more than two roots, then $a=b=c=0$.

**Common mistake:** using $D<0\Rightarrow$ "no roots" when the coefficients are complex. The test needs real coefficients.

See also [[Location of roots]] · [[Quadratic Equations · Formula sheet]]

notes.title: Sum & product of roots, symmetric functions
notes.body:
# Sum & product of roots, symmetric functions
$$\alpha+\beta=-\frac ba,\qquad \alpha\beta=\frac ca$$

**Symmetric functions** (express in $s=\alpha+\beta,\;p=\alpha\beta$)
- $\alpha^2+\beta^2=s^2-2p$
- $(\alpha-\beta)^2=s^2-4p=\dfrac D{a^2}$
- $\alpha^3+\beta^3=s^3-3ps$
- $\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta=\dfrac sp$

**Power sums** $S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n$ satisfy $\;aS_{n+2}+bS_{n+1}+cS_n=0$.
(JEE favourite: $\alpha,\beta$ roots of $x^2-6x-2=0$ and $a_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$ give $\dfrac{a_{10}-2a_8}{2a_9}=3$.)

See also [[Forming equations, transformed roots]] · [[Higher-degree polynomials]]

notes.title: Forming equations, transformed roots
notes.body:
# Forming equations, transformed roots
**From the roots:** $\;x^2-(\text{sum of roots})x+(\text{product of roots})=0$.

**Transformed roots** of $f(x)=0$ (roots $\alpha,\beta$): replace $x$ by the inverse of the transformation.
- Roots $\alpha+k$: $\;f(x-k)=0$
- Roots $k\alpha$: $\;f(x/k)=0$
- Roots $1/\alpha$: $\;f(1/x)=0$, i.e. reverse the coefficients
- Roots $-\alpha$: $\;f(-x)=0$
- Roots $\alpha^2$: put $x\to\sqrt x$ and remove the root sign

**Example.** Roots of $2x^2-3x+1=0$ reciprocated: $x^2-3x+2=0$.

See also [[Sum & product of roots, symmetric functions]]

notes.title: Common roots
notes.body:
# Common roots
For $a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1=0$ and $a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2=0$:

- **One common root:** $\;(c_1a_2-c_2a_1)^2=(a_1b_2-a_2b_1)(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)$, and the root is $\alpha=\dfrac{c_1a_2-c_2a_1}{a_1b_2-a_2b_1}$
- **Both roots common:** $\;\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}=\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$

**Shortcut:** subtract the equations to remove $x^2$, find $\alpha$, then put it back in one equation.

**Common mistake:** when one equation has non-real roots (real coefficients), a common root forces *both* roots common.

See also [[Higher-degree polynomials]]

notes.title: Location of roots
notes.body:
# Location of roots
For $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$, take $a>0$ (else multiply by $-1$). Use three tools: $D$, the sign of $f$ at the given points, the vertex $-\tfrac b{2a}$.

- Both roots $>k$: $\;D\ge0,\; f(k)>0,\; -\tfrac b{2a}>k$
- Both roots $<k$: $\;D\ge0,\; f(k)>0,\; -\tfrac b{2a}<k$
- $k$ between the roots: $\;f(k)<0$ (alone is enough)
- Both roots in $(k_1,k_2)$: $\;D\ge0,\;f(k_1)>0,\;f(k_2)>0,\;k_1<-\tfrac b{2a}<k_2$
- Exactly one root in $(k_1,k_2)$: $\;f(k_1)f(k_2)<0$

**Common mistake:** forgetting the case where the leading coefficient depends on the parameter (check $a=0$ separately).

See also [[Graph & sign of a quadratic, range]] · [[Quadratic inequalities & parameters]]

notes.title: Graph & sign of a quadratic, range
notes.body:
# Graph & sign of a quadratic, range
$$y=a\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2-\frac D{4a},\qquad \text{vertex }\left(-\frac b{2a},\,-\frac D{4a}\right)$$

- $a>0$: opens up, least value $-\tfrac D{4a}$ at $x=-\tfrac b{2a}$
- $a<0$: opens down, greatest value $-\tfrac D{4a}$

**Sign for all $x$**
- $ax^2+bx+c>0\;\forall x\in\mathbb R\iff a>0$ and $D<0$
- $ax^2+bx+c<0\;\forall x\in\mathbb R\iff a<0$ and $D<0$

**Range of $\dfrac{a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1}{a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2}$:** set it equal to $y$, get a quadratic in $x$, demand $D\ge0$ (real $x$).

**Pair of lines:** $ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ factorises into two lines iff $abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2=0$.

See also [[Location of roots]]

notes.title: Higher-degree polynomials
notes.body:
# Higher-degree polynomials
For $a_nx^n+\dots+a_0=0$ with roots $\alpha_i$ (Vieta):
$$\sum\alpha_i=-\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n},\quad \sum_{i<j}\alpha_i\alpha_j=\frac{a_{n-2}}{a_n},\quad \dots,\quad \prod\alpha_i=(-1)^n\frac{a_0}{a_n}$$

**Newton's sums** (monic, $S_k=\sum\alpha_i^k$):
- $1\le k\le n$: $\;S_k+a_{n-1}S_{k-1}+\dots+a_{n-k+1}S_1+k\,a_{n-k}=0$
- $k>n$: $\;S_k+a_{n-1}S_{k-1}+\dots+a_0S_{k-n}=0$

**Facts:** a polynomial of odd degree (real coefficients) has at least one real root; non-real roots come in conjugate pairs; between two roots of $f$ lies a root of $f'$ (Rolle).

See also [[Sum & product of roots, symmetric functions]] · [[Common roots]]

notes.title: Reducible equations (modulus, log, exponential)
notes.body:
# Reducible equations (modulus, log, exponential)
Turn the equation into a quadratic with a substitution, solve, then **go back and check the domain**.

- $|x|$: put $t=|x|\ge0$; reject negative $t$
- $a^{2x}+pa^x+q=0$: put $t=a^x>0$
- $\log$: put $t=\log_a x$; the original needs $x>0$, base $>0$, base $\ne1$
- Reciprocal equations $ax^4+bx^3+cx^2+bx+a=0$: divide by $x^2$, put $t=x+\tfrac1x$ ($|t|\ge2$ for real $x$)
- $(x+a)(x+b)(x+c)(x+d)=k$ with $a+d=b+c$: pair the factors so the $x^2+\dots x$ parts match

**Common mistake:** keeping a root of the quadratic in $t$ that gives no real $x$ (e.g. $t=a^x<0$).

See also [[Quadratic inequalities & parameters]]

notes.title: Quadratic inequalities & parameters
notes.body:
# Quadratic inequalities & parameters
**Solve $ax^2+bx+c>0$** ($a>0$, roots $\alpha<\beta$): $\;x<\alpha$ or $x>\beta$. For $<0$: $\;\alpha<x<\beta$.

**Wavy curve:** put all factors on one side, mark the critical points, alternate signs from the right (watch even powers: no sign change).

**Parameter questions**
- "true for all real $x$" → sign conditions on $a$ and $D$ (see [[Graph & sign of a quadratic, range]])
- "true for all $x$ in an interval" → [[Location of roots]] conditions
- Separate the parameter when possible: $k>g(x)$ for all $x$ $\iff k>\max g$

**Common mistake:** multiplying both sides by an expression whose sign is not known.

See also [[Reducible equations (modulus, log, exponential)]]

notes.title: Indefinite Integration · Formula sheet
notes.body:
The chapter at one glance.

- [[Substitution]]: $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=F(g(x))+C$; $\int\frac{f'}{f}=\ln|f|$
- [[Integration by parts]]: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$; $\int e^x(f+f')=e^xf$
- [[Partial fractions]]: cover-up for linear factors
- [[Trig integrals]]: $t=\tan\tfrac x2$; reduction formulas for $\sin^n,\sec^n,\tan^n$
- [[Irrational functions & Euler substitution]]: the nine special results, Chebyshev's three cases

Always check an answer by differentiating it.

notes.title: Substitution
notes.body:
# Substitution
$$\int f\big(g(x)\big)\,g'(x)\,dx=F\big(g(x)\big)+C$$

**Ready-made forms**
- $\displaystyle\int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$
- $\displaystyle\int[f(x)]^nf'(x)\,dx=\frac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\;(n\ne-1)$
- $\displaystyle\int f(ax+b)\,dx=\frac1aF(ax+b)+C$
- $\displaystyle\int\frac{A\,D+B\,D'}{D}\,dx=Ax+B\ln|D|+C$ (split the numerator as "denominator + its derivative")

**Spot it:** look for a function whose derivative is also present (up to a constant).

**Trick:** $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sin(x-a)\cos(x-b)}$: multiply and divide by $\cos(a-b)$ and write $\cos(a-b)=\cos\big((x-b)-(x-a)\big)$.

See also [[Integration by parts]] · [[Indefinite Integration · Formula sheet]]

notes.title: Integration by parts
notes.body:
# Integration by parts
$$\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du,\qquad \int f(x)g(x)\,dx=f(x)G(x)-\int f'(x)G(x)\,dx$$
Choose $f$ (to differentiate) by **ILATE**: Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential.

**Special forms (no parts needed once you see them)**
- $\displaystyle\int e^x\big(f(x)+f'(x)\big)\,dx=e^xf(x)+C$
- $\displaystyle\int\big(f(x)+xf'(x)\big)\,dx=xf(x)+C$
- $\displaystyle\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)+C$
- $\displaystyle\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}}{a^2+b^2}(a\cos bx+b\sin bx)+C$
- $\displaystyle\int f^{-1}(x)\,dx=xf^{-1}(x)-F\big(f^{-1}(x)\big)+C$

**Common mistake:** applying parts to $\int e^x(\dots)$ without first checking for the $f+f'$ pattern.

See also [[Substitution]] · [[Trig integrals]]

notes.title: Partial fractions
notes.body:
# Partial fractions
For $\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ with $\deg P<\deg Q$ (else divide first):

- Linear factor $(x-a)$: $\;\dfrac A{x-a}$ with $A=\left.\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)/(x-a)}\right|_{x=a}$ (cover-up)
- Repeated $(x-a)^k$: $\;\dfrac{A_1}{x-a}+\dots+\dfrac{A_k}{(x-a)^k}$
- Irreducible quadratic: $\;\dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+px+q}$

**Shortcuts**
- Only even powers of $x$ (e.g. $\frac{x^2}{(x^2+a^2)(x^2+b^2)}$): put $t=x^2$ for the splitting only.
- $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2\pm1}{x^4+kx^2+1}\,dx$: divide by $x^2$, put $t=x\mp\frac1x$.

See also [[Substitution]]

notes.title: Trig integrals
notes.body:
# Trig integrals
**Weierstrass:** $t=\tan\dfrac x2$, $\;\sin x=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2},\;\cos x=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\;dx=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$. Use for $\int\frac{dx}{a+b\cos x}$ and similar.

**$\int\frac{dx}{a\sin^2x+b\cos^2x+c}$:** divide by $\cos^2x$, put $t=\tan x$.

**$\int\frac{p\sin x+q\cos x}{a\sin x+b\cos x}\,dx$:** numerator $=A(\text{den})+B(\text{den})'$.

**Reduction formulas**
- $\displaystyle I_n=\int\sin^nx\,dx=-\frac{\sin^{n-1}x\cos x}{n}+\frac{n-1}nI_{n-2}$
- $\displaystyle I_n=\int\sec^nx\,dx=\frac{\sec^{n-2}x\tan x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}I_{n-2}$
- $\displaystyle I_n+I_{n-2}=\frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1}$ for $I_n=\int\tan^nx\,dx$

See also [[Integration by parts]] · [[Irrational functions & Euler substitution]]

notes.title: Irrational functions & Euler substitution
notes.body:
# Irrational functions & Euler substitution
**The standard results** (complete the square first: $ax^2+bx+c=a\left[\left(x+\frac b{2a}\right)^2+\frac{4ac-b^2}{4a^2}\right]$)
- $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\frac xa$, $\;\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}}=\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}\right|$
- $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\frac x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\frac{a^2}2\sin^{-1}\frac xa$
- $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}\,dx=\frac x2\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}\pm\frac{a^2}2\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2\pm a^2}\right|$

**Linear over root of quadratic:** $px+q=A\dfrac d{dx}(ax^2+bx+c)+B$, then split.

**$\int\frac{dx}{(px+q)\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}}$:** put $px+q=\frac1t$. **$\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+k)\sqrt{x^2+l}}$:** put $x=\frac1t$ or $\sqrt{x^2+l}=xt$.

**Euler substitutions** for $\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}$: $\sqrt{ax^2+bx+c}=t\pm\sqrt a\,x$ ($a>0$), $=xt\pm\sqrt c$ ($c>0$), or $=t(x-\alpha)$ (real root $\alpha$).

**Binomial differential** $\int x^m(a+bx^n)^p\,dx$ is elementary only if one of $p$, $\frac{m+1}n$, $\frac{m+1}n+p$ is an integer (Chebyshev).

See also [[Trig integrals]] · [[Substitution]]
